messages.subject: Feature classes
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Very appreciative of the work behind Wallace!

Is there particular justification for the feature class options currently available in Wallace (i.e., why not all combinations)? I understand there may need to be a limit to the options available for FCs and regularization multipliers for processing purposes, I'm just wondering if the FCs selected have been shown to be more meaningful than others?

Thanks,
Amy

messages.subject: Re: Feature classes
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for using Wallace. The feature class combos available right now are meant to allow increasing levels of complexity. For example, just linear (L) features will produce the simplest response (but with potentially many predictor variables if regularization is low), while LQHP features should produce a very complex response, as hinge features will make it curvilinear and product features will add interactions. In the middle are other options -- LQ is more complex than L, but not as complex as LQH or H. As it is difficult to tell which combo results in the best-fit model, trying a range of these combos is a good idea to start off. We neglected to include threshold features (T) because as Phillips et al. (2017) point out in the maxnet paper, they are kind of like a subset of hinge features and often result in ecologically unrealistic responses. If there is interest, say, in using combos like LP or LQP, we can add these in future versions. However, in our work, the combos we offer are the ones we've found fit the best models for our purposes.

Jamie

Hi Gonzalo:

Problem solved:
- first I was using .asc files without a CRS. Therefor the descriptive variables were "somewhere" in the map but not overlapping with my background. I am now using Erdas .img images and works fine
- second I managed to run rJava using sudo ln -f -s $(/usr/libexec/java_home)/jre/lib/server/libjvm.dylib /usr/local/lib
- I tried to run rJava from Studio, no way (the same message of error), quit RStudio, run terminal, type the common and "voilà" (by the way, previously, it was not working in Windows, neither)

So, thanks a lot for pointing me into the right forum to copy/past the magic command that links rJava with wallace.
All the best,
Agustín

messages.subject: Model predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

My question relates to Wallace, but more directly to the ENMeval package it uses.

If I select "crossvalidate" with 10 replicates in the MaxEnt GUI, the output prediction is given as a mean (and median, min, max) of 10 replicate runs.

For ENMeval, Muscarella et al.(2014) says the "‘random k‐fold’ method [is]...equivalent to the ‘cross‐validate’ partitioning scheme available in the current version of the Maxent software".

So, if I select "random k-fold" with folds=10 in Wallace/ENMeval for a model, is the prediction output also a mean (or some summary) of 10 replicate runs? The ENMeval manual suggests not, that the prediction raster that can be obtained for a given model is on unpartitioned data. So does that mean the prediction is from one replicate using all data?

Or am I misunderstanding?

Thanks,
Amy

messages.subject: Re: Model predictions
messages.body_plain:
Amy,

Yes, sorry for the confusion. ENMeval makes a single random k-fold partition, then does cross validation for those k folds. It does no replicates in the function, but you can do this by simply running ENMevaluate() or the associated module in Wallace again. Hope this answers your question.

Jamie

messages.subject: Bin predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

If I'm understanding correctly, the model outputs called in the Visualize/Project components are from a single run that used all the data points as training samples (no partitioning). I would like to have a model output that incorporates my selected spatial partitioning scheme (e.g., a mean/median of all bins). The individual evaluation bin statistics are provided as output, so is there anyway to get the model predictions from each bin, too?

Thanks,
Amy

messages.subject: Re: Model predictions
messages.body_plain:
Yes, that is correct. The model prediction is always made from the full occurrence dataset in ENMeval. The partitioning and cross validation is done only to make evaluations on test data, and the corresponding statistics are meant to aid the user in selecting optimal model settings. Thus, selection of partition method will not affect the model prediction, just the evaluation statistics.

Jamie

messages.subject: Bin predictions
messages.body_plain:
Amy,

As I wrote in my answer to the previous question, the model objects returned in ENMeval are built from the full occurrence dataset, and the cross validation statistics are meant to help you select the optimal model settings. You cannot retrieve the models built from partitioned occurrence data in an ENMevaluation object, but you could always partition your data in R with ENMeval, run models on each subset, and use raster::predict() to make predictions.

Can I ask why you want an average of the models built from the partitioned datasets? Each of these models has less data than you started with, and theoretically the model with the most data (assuming the occurrences are accurate) should be superior to any model built with a subset. It would help if you could explain your reasoning.

Thanks,

Jamie

messages.subject: Re: Bin predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jamie,

I'm interested in the use of the partitioning as a means of replication, to represent potential variability in the model, response curves, etc. The MaxEnt GUI does this so I assumed ENMeval did the same (which you have previously corrected for me). ENMeval has the useful benefit of non-random options (e.g., block) that the GUI does not. Though I can build the models separately and combine them myself, as you suggest, I wanted to make sure ENMeval couldn't be used to automate some of this (since it presumably makes bin-specific predictions in the background in order to get the cross validation stats?)

I work with invasive species, so value transferability. Spatially-structured model development is one way I'm attempting to mitigate the uncertainty/risk associated with that goal while using MaxEnt. Though I can understand some argument for it, a single model using all points for training seems less robust to me. If you know of a paper that offers reasoning for or against this, I'd definitely be interested.

Thanks,
Amy

You cannot retrieve the models built from partitioned occurrence data in an ENMevaluation object, but you could always partition your data in R with ENMeval, run models on each subset, and use raster::predict() to make predictions.
>
> Can I ask why you want an average of the models built from the partitioned datasets? Each of these models has less data than you started with, and theoretically the model with the most data (assuming the occurrences are accurate) should be superior to any model built with a subset. It would help if you could explain your reasoning.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Jamie

messages.subject: Re: Bin predictions
messages.body_plain:
Amy,

I think I see what your intention is, but let me clarify a bit. The mean test AUC (for example) on spatially structured partitions is meant to demonstrate how well those particular model settings do, given your data, at model transfer to areas with (likely) different environmental characteristics. Summary statistics like this should help you choose which model settings are optimal for your data. Other things you may be interested in are the minimum test AUC, for example, which shows you how bad the worst model was at transfer across all partitions. The new version of ENMeval I'm working on provides these extremes by default.

However, each model made on partitioned data is inadequate by definition, in that it does not include all the available occurrences for your species. If you are trying to model your species' niche as accurately as you can manage, shouldn't you use all the data good enough to model with? The models made on partitioned data are useful for evaluation purposes, but not for estimating the species niche. Averaging them does not seem to me like a better way than using all the data. However, this model average might be useful in order to evaluate transferability in some way. If that was your intention, then I apologize for the long-winded response.

Jamie
